questions.exp: The mnemonic runs C cancer with SCC as m/c, A aspergillosis/autoimmune/abscess, V vascular emboli, I infection with staph and klebsiella, T TB, Y young patients with congenital abnormality. (Book p285)

units.title: The Necrosis-Free Definition of Pneumonia, Its Five Parenchymal Sites, the Necrotising Note, the Six-Step Pathogenesis and the Three Protective Mechanisms
units.sec: The Necrosis-Free Definition of Pneumonia, Its Five Parenchymal Sites, the Necrotising Note, the Six-Step Pathogenesis and the Three Protective Mechanisms
units.guide:
Pneumonia (p274) is acute infection of lung parenchyma without necrosis, seated in alveoli, alveolar and vascular interstitium, respiratory bronchioles and alveolar ducts; necrosis or destruction of parenchyma turns it into necrotising pneumonia or lung abscess.
Pathogenesis runs defective cell-mediated immunity with viral infection → disrupted lung microbiota → alveolar epithelial barrier disruption → bacterial microaspiration → alveoli → IL-1/IL-6/TNFα for fever and IL-8 for neutrophil recruitment → capillary leak → alveolo-capillary exudate → impaired diffusion → hypoxia → dyspnea.
Protective mechanisms are the alveolar macrophage, gag reflex and mucociliary clearance, and the commonest access is the oropharynx via aspiration.

units.title: HAP, VAP and CAP by Source with Their 48-hour Rules, the Lobar and Interstitial Anatomy, the Typical and Atypical Split, and the Four-Part CAP Criteria with Auscultation
units.sec: HAP, VAP and CAP by Source with Their 48-hour Rules, the Lobar and Interstitial Anatomy, the Typical and Atypical Split, and the Four-Part CAP Criteria with Auscultation
units.guide:
HAP occurs >48 hrs after admission and is not present at admission, VAP >48 hrs after endotracheal intubation, and CAP has no timing rule; anatomy splits into lobar and interstitial and organisms into typical and atypical (p275).
CAP requires an acute infection <1 week with cardinal features — fever, dyspnea/tachypnea/tachycardia, cough ± sputum, pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis — plus infiltrates on CXR or CT and no other explanation.
Auscultation gives bronchial breath sounds and crackles, which the page labels subjective.

units.title: The Lobular and Interstitial Organism Columns, the MRSA-in-India Note and the Seven-Row Typical against Atypical Table
units.sec: The Lobular and Interstitial Organism Columns, the MRSA-in-India Note and the Seven-Row Typical against Atypical Table
units.guide:
Lobar pneumonia (p276) is restricted to one lobe with Strep pneumoniae most common, Staph aureus including MRSA, Klebsiella, H. influenzae and Moraxella; the interstitial column opens with virus as most common, then mycoplasma, chlamydia and Legionella with features of both, then Aspergillus, PCP in HIV and Nocardia in the immunocompromised.
The note states MRSA is not common in India.
Typical against atypical runs extracellular vs intracellular, abrupt vs insidious, alveolar capillary exudates vs interstitial infiltrates, neutrophilic vs lymphocytic, detectable vs undetectable on culture, raised CRP/procalcitonin/leucocytosis vs none, and large lobar consolidation vs bilateral patchy interstitial change.

units.title: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart
units.sec: Community Acquired MRSA, the Outpatient to ICU Organism Shift, MRSA and MDR Risk within Three Months, and Pneumococcal Morphology, Culture and Haemolysis Chart
units.guide:
Community acquired MRSA (p277) is suggested by concurrent influenza or by cavity with hemoptysis and pneumatocele.
Outpatients carry strep pneumoniae, virus, mycoplasma, chlamydia and H. influenzae; non-ICU inpatients strep pneumoniae from low CMI, respiratory viruses and Legionella; ICU patients strep pneumoniae, MRSA and MDR gram-negative with high mortality — MRSA and MDR risk being CCF, hemodialysis, antibiotics and hospitalization within the last 3 months, and structural lung disease.
Pneumococci are gram-positive diplococci in chains, flame-shaped or lanceolate, alpha hemolytic with partial hemolysis on 5% blood agar, green colour and a draughtsman/carrom coin colony; complete hemolysis means streptococcus, partial means pneumoniae or viridans, and none means enterococci.

units.title: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes
units.sec: Pneumococcus against Viridans, the Four Toxins, the Quellung Reaction, Type 3 Invasiveness and the CAP Risk and Poor-Prognosis Notes
units.guide:
Strep pneumoniae is bile soluble, optochin susceptible and inulin fermenting while viridans is negative in all three (p278).
The toxins are capsular polysaccharide, pneumolysin (cytolytic, punching pores in the membrane), IgA1 and pneumococcal somatic C antigen, which precipitates C reactive protein; the Quellung reaction shows swelling of the capsule, and S. pneumoniae is non-invasive except type 3.
CAP risk comes from deficient CMI — diabetes, chronic kidney disease, hemodialysis, COPD, bronchiectasis, cardiac failure and age >65 — or from immunocompromise by steroids/monoclonals, transplant and neutropenia, and poor prognosis is marked by hypothermia and leukopenia with atypical organisms.

units.title: Type 2 Alveolar Binding, the Lobar Pneumonia Cardinal and Abdominal Symptoms, the Older-Patient Caveat, Resolution Timing and the Four-Column Chest Film Table
units.sec: Type 2 Alveolar Binding, the Lobar Pneumonia Cardinal and Abdominal Symptoms, the Older-Patient Caveat, Resolution Timing and the Four-Column Chest Film Table
units.guide:
Bacteria bind type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (p279); lobar pneumonia has cardinal high spiking fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough, hemoptysis and dyspnea, with abdominal pain and hiccups or confusion added, and in the elderly confusion may be the only symptom while classical signs are absent.
Fever and leukocytosis resolve 4–5 days after antibiotics; blood shows leucocytosis, raised CRP and procalcitonin in lobar disease against normal values in interstitial bronchopneumonia.
Films separate into lobar (homogeneous consolidation, silhouette sign, air bronchogram, sharply marginated fissure, usually pneumococcus), bronchopneumonia (poorly defined heterogeneous patchy infiltrates with air bronchogram, staph giving multilobar disease with cavitation, pneumatoceles and abscess), interstitial (bilateral diffuse fine reticular opacity, PCP) and aspiration (airspace opacification, gravity dependent, after stroke or seizure).

units.title: Sputum and Blood Culture Yields, BAL, and the Fourteen-Row Etiology Table from Bacteraemia to Atherosclerosis
units.sec: Sputum and Blood Culture Yields, BAL, and the Fourteen-Row Etiology Table from Bacteraemia to Atherosclerosis
units.guide:
Sputum microscopy and culture are done in atypical pneumonia, blood culture has poor yield and BAL is listed last (p280).
The etiology table pairs bacteremia/diabetes with S. pneumoniae; alcoholism, upper lobe involvement, bulging fissure, cavitation and golden S with Klebsiella; COPD/smoking/bronchiectasis with Pseudomonas; cystic fibrosis with Burkholderia cepacia; lung abscess with MRSA and anaerobes; cavity with MRSA; pneumatocele with Klebsiella; dementia or low consciousness with anaerobes.
Exposures pair sheep, cats and goats with Coxiella, rabbits with Francisella, bats with Histoplasma, cruise ships with Legionella, the Ohio and St. Lawrence valleys with Histoplasma capsulatum and atherosclerosis with Chlamydia pneumoniae.

units.title: Extrapulmonary Mycoplasma, and the Air Bronchogram, Silhouette, Golden S and Mediastinal Shift Captions
units.sec: Extrapulmonary Mycoplasma, and the Air Bronchogram, Silhouette, Golden S and Mediastinal Shift Captions
units.guide:
Mycoplasma adds cold antibody autoimmune hemolysis, Steven Johnson's syndrome and Guillain Barre syndrome (p281).
An air bronchogram is air-filled space within consolidation, not specific and also seen in cardiogenic pulmonary edema; left lower lobe consolidation loses the left heart silhouette with an intact diaphragm, while right upper lobe disease loses the ascending aorta silhouette.
Golden S/reverse S and the bulging fissure sign are bracketed to Klebsiella, and collapse shifts the mediastinum to the same side.

units.title: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule
units.sec: Mycoplasma against Legionella Films, the Fibrocalcific Scar, Necrotising Klebsiella and the Pneumatocele Cascade with Its 4 mm Rule
units.guide:
Captions on p282 read mycoplasma/chlamydia minimal interstitial infiltrates misdiagnosed as a normal study, Legionella bilateral dense consolidation, bronchopneumonia air space opacification, and a fibrocalcific scar post TB with fibrosis; necrotising Klebsiella shows upper lobe involvement and a bulging fissure.
The pneumatocele cascade runs dense white opacity → focal suppurative abscess → necrosis and destruction → rupture into bronchus → air entry → gas within consolidation inside a wall of minimum 4 mm → air-fluid levels → cavity.
Pneumatoceles occur in IV drug abusers and after viral infection, progress to cavity, associate with MRSA and measure <4 mm, while a bulla is a cavity >4 mm.

units.title: The CURB-65 Score with Its BUN and Blood Urea Equivalents, the BTS Outpatient Algorithm and the Non-Severe against Severe Inpatient Antibiotic Table
units.sec: The CURB-65 Score with Its BUN and Blood Urea Equivalents, the BTS Outpatient Algorithm and the Non-Severe against Severe Inpatient Antibiotic Table
units.guide:
CURB-65 (p283) is confusion, urea >7 mmol/L (BUN ≈21 mg/dL, blood urea ≈42 mg/dL), respiratory rate >30/min, blood pressure <90 systolic or <60 diastolic and age ≥65, scoring 0 for outpatient, 1–2 for inpatient and ≥3 for ICU care.
The BTS outpatient arm without resistance risk gives amoxicillin 1 g TDS plus azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg days 2–5 or clarithromycin 500 mg BD, or amoxicillin plus doxycycline; with resistance risk it gives amoxyclav 625 mg TDS plus azithromycin or doxycycline, cephalosporins being an alternative.
Inpatients take a β-lactam (ampicillin + sulbactam 1.5 g QID IV or piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g QID IV) plus a macrolide 500 mg BD, second line levofloxacin 750 mg/day, and severe ICU disease a β-lactam plus levofloxacin without fluoroquinolone monotherapy.

units.title: MRSA Cover and the 48–72-hour Response Rule, Empyema, Lung Abscess and ARDS, the Empyema against Abscess Table and the Definition of a Lung Cavity
units.sec: MRSA Cover and the 48–72-hour Response Rule, Empyema, Lung Abscess and ARDS, the Empyema against Abscess Table and the Definition of a Lung Cavity
units.guide:
MRSA cover follows isolation, recent hospitalization or prior MRSA, and response is judged at 48–72 hours, with no response meaning a complication and CT (p284).
Empyema is macroscopic pus with a complicated parapneumonic effusion, diagnosed by the CT split pleura sign with thickened pleura and ↑protein, ↑LDH, ↓glucose and treated by intercostal drainage; lung abscess is destruction with cavity and takes vancomycin + meropenem + clindamycin for 6–8 weeks; ARDS with MDR and metastatic infection complete the list.
Empyema against abscess is smooth vs irregular wall, obtuse vs acute angle, lentiform vs rounded on X-ray and positive vs negative split pleura sign, a simple synpneumonic effusion being sterile; a cavity is a gas-filled space within consolidation, mass or nodule from expectorated necrotic debris, seen in staphylococcus and klebsiella.

units.title: The Bulla, Cyst and Thin-Walled Cavity Captions, the Four Thick-Walled Causes and the Seven-Letter CAVITY Mnemonic
units.sec: The Bulla, Cyst and Thin-Walled Cavity Captions, the Four Thick-Walled Causes and the Seven-Letter CAVITY Mnemonic
units.guide:
The caption strip on p285 shows a bulla, a cyst and a thin walled cavity, then thick walled cavities.
Thick walled cavities are abscess, necrotising SCC, Wegener's granulomatosis and blastomycosis.
The CAVITY mnemonic gives C cancer with SCC most common, A aspergillosis/autoimmune (Wegener's)/abscess, V vascular emboli, I infection with Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella, T TB, Y young patients with congenital abnormality, and fungus as Cryptococcus, Aspergillus and Coccidioidomycosis.
